dataset.name: ESS-DIVE Reporting Format for Hydrologic Monitoring Data and Metadata
description: The ESS-DIVE Reporting Format (RF) for Hydrologic Monitoring Data and Metadata was designed for water level, temperature, electrical conductivity, specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, and pH measured in situ using sensors deployed in water bodies. It can also be applied to a broader suite of variables beyond its original scope. The RF is intended to provide clear and easy guidance to data generators aiming to upload consistent findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) datasets. The RF includes instructions (pdf), a term guide (csv), templates (csv and xlsx), and a list of recommended vocabulary (csv) to equip the data generator with all of the tools needed to successfully apply the RF. There is also a crosswalk to some key data resources and standards (csv). Users should cite this dataset when using the RF but are encouraged to access the RF files on GitHub (https://github.com/ess-dive-community/essdive-hydrologic-monitoring) where the RF documentation is maintained and updated on the ESS-DIVE Community Space GitHub. Questions and suggestions for improvement can be submitted as GitHub issues.

measurementTechnique:
The creation of the ESS-DIVE Reporting Format (RF) for Hydrologic Monitoring included iterative stages of research, drafting, discussion, and revising. The initial research phase included a review of existing hydrologic monitoring data sources and repositories, reporting formats, and standards. This review included such resources as the US Geological Survey, Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Science (CUAHSI), National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Water Quality Portal, US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Sustaining the Earth's Watersheds-Agricultural Research Data System (STEWARDS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Estuarine Research Reserve, Stroud Water Center, Smithsonian Marine Global Earth Observatory (MarineGEO), Observations Data Model (ODM) 1 and 2, and others. We collected information on the guidance outlined across the reviewed resources and when applicable, downloaded data sets to evaluate the structures in practice. For a detailed summary of how some of the key existing resources and standards map to the RF, see the data standards crosswalk (HydroRF_Crosswalk.csv).
The initial research phase also included discussions with hydrologic monitoring data generators to understand their existing practices and what they would find useful in the RF. After the initial research phase, we created a preliminary draft RF, discussed with data generators and data users, including modelers, and iterated on the draft. Over the span of drafting the RF, we held discussions with 35 people across the USGS, CUAHSI, Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments (SPRUCE), Oak Ridge National Laboratory Mercury Science Focus Area (SFA), Argonne National Laboratory Wetland Biogeochemistry SFA, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Watershed Function ESS SFA, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory River Corridor SFA, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory Biogeochemistry of Actinides SFA, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory Groundwater Quality SFA, Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, Smithsonian MarineGEO, ESS-DIVE, Ameriflux, Worldwide Hydrobiogeochemistry Observation Network for Dynamic River Systems (WHONDRS), IDEAS Watershed Project, and individual researchers from universities, private industry, and national laboratories. We also received feedback through presentations at the U.S. Department of Energy Environmental System Science (ESS) Cyberinfrastructure Meeting (May 2020), ESS-DIVE Monthly Webinar (August 2020), and the ESS-DIVE Annual Community Data Workshop (May 2021).
